description: We are Zenacor, a team from Salt Lake City, Utah. Some interests and skills that are present among our members are computer science, graphic design, and generally space!
summary: Artemis Assist is a browser tool that answers the question that every south pole mission encounters. At this site, on these dates, will we have sunlight for power and will the Earth be in view for direct communication? Our application combines JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions with terrain data traced from NASA’s LOLA elevation data, for terrain awareness in landing zones and light illumination. Users can choose a mission and see all nine Artemis III candidate regions, or any custom site, ranked by solar power, Earth contact, and longest dark spell. A 3D tier system of specific site terrain, moon surface visualization, and scaled earth/sun/moon view are enabled so that users can test sites and plan missions. Buttons and side-by-side comparison show how a one-day to two-week delay changes results, even including a scrub for light and shadow diffusion across terrain. Our results match NASA’s long-term illumination maps within about two percentage points on average, accounting for drastic changes across several regions (e.g., light). The model covers 2027 and has great potential to expand. Planners get what once took Horizons, Quickmap, and Moon Trek all together, just in a few clicks using Artemis Assist, so mission plans can be now scoped and edited with ease.
details:
Artemis Assist is a web based application that assists users in planning missions based upon date, sunlight, direct communication with earth and solar power. The user can specify a mission window between 1 hour and 60 days of any given date in 2027. The application instantly provides a ranking for all nine Artemis III candidate locations or any desired location on the moon. The application provides:

  • Time in sunlight, average solar power and maximum period of darkness.
  • Time in view of earth, communication gap time and time in view of both sun and earth.
  • 3D view of landscape and a panoramic view of the horizon with the sun and earth rising and setting behind realistic crater edges and mountains.

This application uses lots of data and information provided by NASA. NASA’s JPL Horizons has been used to provide information about the sun and earth (azimuth/elevation every hour of 2027), LOLA Elevation Data has been used to create a landscape view of the horizon for each location.

The sun has been assumed as a 0.53 degree diameter circle. Partial sunlight has therefore been assumed as partial solar power. If any part of the earth appears above the landscape then it will be assumed that there is communication. Each location is scored between 0-1 depending on how much solar power is available (45%), how much of earth is visible (30%) and keeping the maximum darkness to a minimum (25%).

Overall, Artemis Assist can easily and clearly be summarised as providing all the information from JPL Horizons, QuickMap and Moon Trek in a matter of clicks. This information has been displayed in an easy to understand format using simple graphs to help educators and students understand the information alongside specialists. All regions are automatically re-ranked depending on the mission window set. Simple features have been added to make the application easy to use such as slip buttons. Locations can be compared next to each other with each feature matching up. If the period of darkness or communication gap increases past a certain limit specified by the user this will be flagged. It can also provide an estimate of possible lift off times from the 16 actual launch sites on earth.

We aim to make the initial screening of Lunar landing sites faster. We want to make the trade-off between lighting and communication for the south pole landings easy to understand. This can also be used to highlight the challenges that the south pole of the moon poses to humanity due to the low sun angle, long shadows and earth being close to the horizon. This application can be used by mission planners and members of the general public. As small changes to the site/date can determine if a mission is possible this helps identify any risks early. This broad audience means that this application will be relevant to a multitude of people and has great potential for development in the future. Future development could include rocket trajectory planning and a stronger algorithm.

What makes Artemis Assist Creative is its three linked zoom levels, from the Sun, Earth, and Moon system, down to a single crater rim, running all on one clock. Visibility is judged against real terrain, rather than just off a smooth Moon, and a Launch planner works backwards, from the landing to the lift off.

Tech Stack:

  • Front-end: Next.js and React using TypeScript. Tailwind CSS was used for styling. Zustand was used for managing application state.
  • 3D: Three.js using React Three Fiber and drei.
  • Back-end: Using Next.js API routes to provide cached data from JPL Horizons for custom locations.
  • Data Processing: Geotiff.js has been used to convert LOLA elevation data into landscape horizons. Python has been used (NumPy, Pillow) to create moon textures.
  • Data: JPL Horizons to provide sun/earth data. LRO LOLA elevation data provided by NASA Goddard for landscape/horizon. NASA’s Moon Trek for imagery/links. NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit and Blue Marble for moon/earth globes. USGS Artemis III region outlines for the nine candidate locations.

We validated our model by comparing it to NASA’s published long term illumination study (Mazarico et al., 2011). On average across all nine locations the difference between our model and NASA’s was within 2.0 percentage points for the sun and 1.9 percentage points for the earth. For Nobile Rim 2 the difference between the models was within around 1% for the sun and around 0.1% for the earth.

This was created on laptops using GitHub for version control. AI coding tools were used (see AI usage section).

No special hardware was used.

Factors to consider whilst creating this application were mainly accuracy and limitations. The terrain data used was 80metres and the model only covers 2027. NASA’s maps are long term averages. We aimed this at mission planners for potential launches, educators and the general public. Therefore most of the language used was simple and easy to understand. A short tutorial was included to guide the user around the website and how to use our application in general. This made it easy to understand regardless of who reads it as the people who will and/or may interact with this application vary greatly in their knowledge of the technical aspects.
